summary.text: 要 is traditionally interpreted as a picture of a person holding the waist. The graph was used for “waist”; its common “want” and “need” uses are proposed to come from reusing it for a different word thought to have sounded similar.

formation.text: Pictographic under the whole-scene interpretation: the early graph depicts a person holding the body's middle. Competing analyses disagree about the upper and hand-like forms, so the present shape should not be confidently split into modern-looking parts. The Han dictionary's analysis involving 𦥑 and phonetic 交省 is an ancient interpretation, not a settled account of the graph's construction.

history.text: 要 is recorded in Shang oracle-bone and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, followed by later forms. The listed inscription examples establish an early record of the graph, but not which words those tokens represented. The curated seal-script image is a modern rendering, not an ancient artifact.

Early analyses differ: one reads the graph as a person or woman holding the waist as a whole picture; others parse forms involving 女, hands, or 臼. The Han dictionary instead describes 𦥑 and 交省, with the latter as a sound element. These interpretations do not establish a shared component breakdown.

要 is described as the original graph for the waist word later written 腰, formed by adding 肉 to distinguish the body-part word. This is a proposed history of 腰's written form; 腰 is not a component of 要.

uncertainties.text: The proposed borrowing for “want” and “need” has no dated borrowing event or independently verified early example in the evidence here. The old word's name and the historical sound match are not established.
A pathway from “waist” through “pivot” or “essential” to “need” and “want” has been proposed, but the evidence does not establish this chronology or connect the senses in sequence.

The early graph's component identities remain disputed; the cited paleographic analyses are reported secondhand, and the listed inscription forms were not visually inspected in the research summarized here.

senses.period: dating unresolved; attested in transmitted pre-imperial texts
senses.text: Transmitted pre-imperial works use 要 for the waist. These examples attest the sense but do not establish its earliest date.

The familiar “want” and “need” uses are explained as a proposed borrowing: the sign used for “waist” was reused to write a different word thought to sound similar. This is not established as a meaning change from “waist.”
要 has these current uses, but the evidence does not establish when they arose or how they relate historically to the waist or want/need uses.

limitations.text: The inscription list establishes an early graphic record, not the word represented by each token. The waist use is attested in transmitted texts, but its earliest occurrence is undated.
The borrowing account is proposed; no dated event or early “want/need” example is established here, and the old word's name and sound are unknown.
The sources do not establish a chronological pathway among the waist, pivot, essential, need, desire, obligation, and imminent-future uses.

evidence.text: A woman 女 with hands on her waist 覀
Pictograph of two hands grabbing a woman's waist. The current meaning "want" is a phonetic loan. The original meaning "waist" is now written as 腰.
身中也。象人要自𦥑之形。从𦥑，交省聲。

Pictogram (象形): a man 大 then drawn as a woman (女) with two hands pointing to his/her midsection. On top of the character there was huge eye 目, then stylized as a horn 角. The hands gradually shifted upwards; hence, a nearly-original version of the character is 𡢗. All the upper part was eventually stylized as 覀. Unrelated to 栗 but partly related to 票.
Original meaning was “waist” (now 腰 (OC *qew)).

evidence.text: The study lists 要 in Shang oracle-bone examples, including 合集8175, and in Western Zhou bronze examples, including 是要簋 and 伯要敦; it also lists Spring and Autumn, Warring States, Qin, and Han-period forms. Its analysis describes the oracle graph as 女 with two hands and a head-like upper element, and reports competing component analyses: Li Xiaoding rejects 交 as phonetic and reads the graph as a woman holding her waist; another cited proposal treats it as a compound involving 臼/女. The author concludes 要 is the original graph for 腰, with 肉 later added to distinguish the body-part word. These are scholarly interpretations, not a visually inspected glyph in this research.

evidence.field: graphic history and Old Chinese comparisons
evidence.text: The entry reproduces Western Zhou bronze and small-seal forms and identifies 𡢗 and 𡚩 as alternative forms. It lists Zhengzhang 2003 *qew for 要 and 腰 and Baxter–Sagart 2014 for 要: Middle Chinese ‹ʔjiewᴴ›, Old Chinese *[q]ew(k)-s, glossed “important.” These B–S values agree with the supplied local 要 row; that row is explicitly the MC/Tone-H form and is not interchangeable with the level-tone reading or the Zhengzhang system.
evidence.title: 要 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: This entry cites Guo Yongbing, “談古文字中的‘要’字和從‘要’之字,” 古文字研究 28 (2010), pp. 108–115. It describes senses including pivot/essential point and necessity. This records a competing scholarly interpretation; the full cited article was not inspected here.

Supplied local rows give current Mandarin 要 yào and 女 nǚ, plus Baxter–Sagart entries for 要 and 女, but no official character-page click-through could be verified here. Those local rows are not external evidence and do not establish an ancient phonetic relationship.

evidence.text: The supplied Baxter–Sagart 2014 rows give 女 MC nrjoX, OC *nraʔ (female) and a separate nǜ row MC nrjoH, OC *nraʔ-s (give as a wife); 要 is MC 'jiewH, OC *[q]ew(k)-s, gloss important. The row notation separates senses and tones; it does not support treating 女 as a phonetic component of 要. No historical phonetic role for 女 is established by the component analyses inspected.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

search_audit.outcome: Search returned general database documentation and unrelated records rather than an exact 要 record. The attempted Xiaoxuetang query URLs were inaccessible and were not used as evidence or image candidates.

gaps: The primary cited 2010 article by 郭永秉 was not accessed; the conflicting graph analyses are recorded through a secondary source and a separate paleographic study.

No independently verified oracle-bone or bronze occurrence for the word sense “want/need” was found. Do not infer its chronology from a modern gloss list; the textual citations inspected substantiate waist meaning only.
The exact date and semantic pathway from waist to pivot/essential, necessity, desire, obligation, and future use remain unestablished in the inspected sources.

The graph's upper and hand-like elements are disputed. No glyph image was visually inspected in this research; do not assert details such as an eye, horn, or hands shifting upward as established graphic chronology.

The source for the presumed borrowing relationship between the waist word written 要 and other 要 senses was not inspected in full. Evidence supports an established lexicographic proposal, not a demonstrated dated borrowing event.

The codepoint-specific Unicode Unihan records for 要 and 腰 failed to load. The local exact 要 rows were checked as supplied, but an official character-page click-through was not verified; no local row was used as external proof.

The cited primary 2010 article by 郭永秉 was not accessed; competing structural interpretations are supported here by the scholarly study's references to Li Xiaoding and Lu Shixian and by secondary reporting, not by inspection of that article.

The upper and hand-like elements of early 要 are disputed. The sources support reporting proposed analyses but do not establish an uncontested component-by-component interpretation. No component can confidently be classified as a phonetic element on the evidence inspected; the Shuowen 交省聲 explanation is an ancient dictionary analysis, not verified historical sound evidence.

The sources inspected do not date the first waist-word occurrence, establish which senses in the modern dictionary list came first, or demonstrate a dated borrowing event from a waist word into want/need or other meanings. A waist-to-pivot-to-essential pathway remains an unverified semantic proposal.

Although the scholarly study lists Shang and Western Zhou graphic exemplars, this research did not inspect their source artifacts directly. The study's inscription list does not establish the lexical reading of each particular token.

The official Unicode codepoint records for 要, 女 and 腰 returned internal errors. The harness-provided local readings were checked for notation and provenance but are not cited as externally verified readings.

The seal-script image is an identified, reusable modern vector redraw. No exact, inspected direct-image page for a usable inscriptional glyph was established in this run; Commons' linked Shang and Zhou alternatives led to category pages rather than a verified 要 file.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; modern digital rendering of a historical script form, not a dated artifact image
items.caption: A modern rendering of 要 in Shuowen seal-script style. The Shuowen account interprets the character as the body's middle and describes a person holding the waist, while analyses of the earlier graph remain disputed.
items.alt: Black seal-script style glyph with a tall central form containing two openings, flanked by curved strokes on both sides.
items.selection_reason: This identified seal-script rendering offers a useful visual reference for 要's historical form; its accompanying historical interpretation is explicitly uncertain, and the cited study reports Shang and Western Zhou examples alongside competing analyses.
items.rights: Commons page states that the SVG representation is public domain; the file page also records that its digital source was Richard Sears, with courtesy permission. Modern vector redraw.

limitations.text: This is a modern vector redraw, not an ancient inscription image, and cannot settle the disputed interpretation of the early graph. The cited study lists early inscription examples but does not establish what word each specific inscription records.
